summary: Describes the changes to OSPF needed to support IPv6. The fundamental mechanisms, including flooding, designated router election, areas, and SPF calculations, stay the same. Changes were needed because of differences in protocol semantics between IPv4 and IPv6 and to handle the larger addresses. It replaced RFC 2740 and has been updated several times.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5340 defines OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3), the version of the OSPF routing protocol that runs over IPv6. Routers still share news about their links the same way they did with IPv4, but addresses now appear only in separate advertisements, so the protocol core works with any network protocol. This matters because it is the specification that made OSPF usable on IPv6 networks.

what is a link lsa in ospfv3
subtitle: The OSPF link-state routing protocol adjusted to run over IPv6.

tldr.problem: OSPF for IPv4 carries IPv4 addresses inside its packets and its core advertisements, so it cannot carry IPv6 routes unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv3 keeps flooding, Designated Router election, areas and SPF calculation, but strips addresses out of packets and the basic LSAs, runs per link instead of per subnet, adds new LSA types for IPv6 prefixes, and leaves authentication to IPsec.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 2740 as the specification of OSPF for IPv6. It has not been obsoleted, but five later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 5340 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2740. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6845, RFC 6860, RFC 7503, RFC 8362 and RFC 9454, so it should be read together with those updates.

sections.title: OSPF for IPv6 in Brief
sections.content:
RFC 5340 describes the modifications needed to run OSPF over version 6 of the Internet Protocol (IPv6). The fundamental mechanisms of OSPF stay unchanged: flooding, Designated Router (DR) election, area support and Shortest Path First (SPF) calculations. Some changes were still necessary, either because protocol semantics differ between IPv4 and IPv6 or simply to handle the larger IPv6 addresses, and these changes raise the protocol version from 2 to 3. OSPF for IPv6 is also called OSPF version 3 (OSPFv3).

Neighbor discovery with Hello packets, adjacency formation, the interface and neighbor state machines, the link types (point-to-point, broadcast, NBMA, point-to-multipoint and virtual links) and LSA aging all remain as in OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328). OSPFv3 runs directly over IPv6 and supports the optional capabilities of OSPF for IPv4, including demand circuit support and Not-So-Stubby Areas (NSSAs). Even with larger addresses, most OSPFv3 packets are almost as compact as their OSPFv2 counterparts.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv3 is OSPF adjusted to work with IPv6. Routers still discover neighbors, elect a designated router, and share link-state news in the same way; only the parts that carried IPv4 addresses changed.

sections.title: What Changed from OSPF for IPv4
sections.content:
The RFC groups the differences from OSPF for IPv4 (RFC 2328) into several themes.

  • Per link, not per subnet. IPv6 allows several prefixes on one link, and two nodes can talk directly over a link even when they do not share a common IPv6 prefix, so OSPF now runs per link instead of per IP subnet.
  • No addressing in the core. IPv6 addresses appear only in LSA payloads carried by Link State Update packets. Router IDs, Area IDs and Link State IDs stay 32 bits wide and can no longer be assigned as IPv6 addresses. Neighboring routers are always identified by Router ID.
  • Flooding scope. The LS type field now codes three flooding scopes: link-local, area and AS.
  • Instance ID. Multiple OSPF instances can run on one link, for example on a network access point segment shared by several providers.
  • Link-local addresses. OSPF packets are sent from the interface's link-local address, except on virtual links, where a global-scope address MUST be used. Link-local addresses MUST NOT be advertised in inter-area-prefix-LSAs, AS-external-LSAs, NSSA-LSAs or intra-area-prefix-LSAs.
  • Authentication removed. The AuType and Authentication fields are gone from the packet header; OSPFv3 relies on IPv6's own security protocols instead.

The Options field in Hello and Database Description packets grows to 24 bits. An address is expressed as a prefix plus length rather than an address plus mask, so the default route is a prefix of length 0. The Router ID 0.0.0.0 is reserved and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 addresses now appear only in separate advertisements, not in the protocol's own packets or in the basic topology records. Each record also carries a scope label saying how far it should be shared, and an instance number so several OSPF domains can share one link.

sections.title: Packets and the Hello Packet
sections.content:
OSPFv3 runs directly over IPv6 with Next Header value 89. There are five packet types, and all of them start with a standard 16-byte header holding the version (3), the packet type, the packet length, the source's Router ID, the Area ID, an IPv6 upper-layer checksum and the Instance ID. A received packet whose Instance ID does not match the receiving interface's Instance ID is discarded.

Hello packets are sent to the multicast address FF02::5 (AllSPFRouters), and some flooding packets go to FF02::6 (AllDRouters). These are link-local-scope addresses, and the IPv6 Hop Limit of packets sent to them should be 1. Where routers map the IPv6 Traffic Class to a Differentiated Services Code Point, OSPFv3 packets SHOULD be sent with DSCP CS6.

The Hello packet no longer carries any address information. It now includes an Interface ID that the originating router assigns to identify its interface to the link, used as the network-LSA's Link State ID if the router becomes DR. It also carries the router priority, the 24-bit Options, the HelloInterval, the RouterDeadInterval, and the Designated Router and Backup Designated Router identified by Router ID (0.0.0.0 when there is none). Routers on a link must agree on HelloInterval and RouterDeadInterval, or they will not form neighbor relationships.
sections.plainLanguage: Every OSPFv3 message begins with the same 16-byte header. Routers send hello messages to a shared multicast address on their link, stating their identity and timing settings; a router that hears a hello with different timing settings will not become a neighbor.

sections.title: Link State Advertisements
sections.content:
All LSAs begin with a common 20-byte header: LS Age, LS Type, Link State ID, Advertising Router, LS Sequence Number, LS Checksum and Length. The 16-bit LS type has three generic bits above an LSA function code. The U-bit says how to treat an unknown LSA type: 0 means treat it as if it had link-local flooding scope, 1 means store and flood it as if the type were understood. The S2 and S1 bits code the flooding scope: 00 is link-local, 01 is area, 10 is AS, and 11 is reserved.

Addressing semantics have been removed from the router-LSA and the network-LSA, which now describe topology only. A router's interface information may be spread across several router-LSAs, and receivers MUST treat all router-LSAs from one router as an aggregate during the SPF calculation. Prefix information lives in other LSA types. Intra-area-prefix-LSAs carry the prefixes that in IPv4 were included in router-LSAs and network-LSAs. Type 3 and type 4 summary-LSAs are renamed inter-area-prefix-LSAs and inter-area-router-LSAs. AS-external-LSAs and NSSA-LSAs carry external prefixes, with an optional forwarding address and route tag; they can also reference another LSA for route attributes outside the scope of OSPF.

The new link-LSA has link-local scope and is never flooded past its link. It has three purposes: it gives the router's link-local address to the other routers on the link, it lists the IPv6 prefixes to associate with the link, and it advertises the Options bits to be used in the network-LSA for the link. For network-LSAs and link-LSAs the Link State ID is the originator's Interface ID, and these are the only LSAs whose size cannot be limited: a network-LSA MUST list all routers on the link, and a link-LSA MUST list all of the router's addresses on the link. The Options field of a network-LSA is the logical OR of the Options advertised by each router on the link in its link-LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers write records about their surroundings. Some records stay on one link, some travel through one area, and some travel through the whole routing domain; the record's type field states which. Topology and address lists are now kept in separate records, so one record can grow or change without rewriting the other.

sections.title: Flooding and Route Calculation
sections.content:
Most flooding rules are as in OSPFv2, but which interfaces are eligible to flood an LSA now depends on its scope. AS-scoped LSAs go out every interface except virtual links, and AS-external-LSAs are not flooded into stub or NSSA areas. A self-originated LSA is simply one whose Advertising Router is the router's own Router ID. When an LSA's contents change, the parts of the routing table that must be recalculated depend on the LSA's type: changes to router-LSAs, network-LSAs, intra-area-prefix-LSAs or link-LSAs force a full recalculation, while changes to the other types allow incremental work.

The routing table calculation follows the five steps of OSPFv2. The graph's vertices are routers, identified by Router ID, and transit links, identified by the DR's Interface ID plus its Router ID. Instead of reading stub networks out of router-LSAs, the router examines the area's intra-area-prefix-LSAs; the cost of a prefix is its advertised metric plus the cost to the router or transit link the LSA references. A prefix with the NU-bit set SHOULD NOT be included in the routing calculation.

Next hops are link-local addresses taken from the neighbor's link-LSA, which is needed on link types such as NBMA where the two routers need not exchange Hellos. Virtual links must use global-scope addresses, AS-scoped LSAs are never flooded over them, and a link-LSA SHOULD NOT be originated for a virtual link because it has no link-local address or associated prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record is shared only as far as its scope label allows. Every router then computes the shortest paths across the area, and attaches the address lists from the separate prefix records to learn how to reach each destination.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 2740
sections.content:
RFC 5340 obsoletes RFC 2740. Implementations of RFC 2740 fully interoperate with this specification, and all additions and changes are backward compatible.

  • Support for multiple interfaces on the same link, only partly specified before, is now complete. One Active Interface sends and receives OSPF control traffic while the others become Standby Interfaces, with a new Standby interface state. A router detects the situation when it receives a Hello carrying one of its own link-local addresses with a different Interface ID.
  • MOSPF (Multicast Extensions to OSPF) for IPv6 is deprecated. The RFC states there are no known implementations, and the associated bits and LSA type are freed for reassignment.
  • An NSSA specification unique to OSPFv3 is included, which together with RFC 3101 provides enough detail to implement the function.
  • The old restriction on flooding unknown LSAs into stub and NSSA areas is deprecated: link and area scope LSAs with U-bit 1 now flood through those areas.
  • A LinkLSASuppression interface parameter allows suppressing link-LSAs on interfaces that are not broadcast or NBMA.
  • The DN-bit is added to the prefix options, MOSPF-related bits are deprecated, and all references to IPv6 site-local addresses are removed.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is the consolidated rulebook for OSPFv3. Routers built to the earlier specification still work with routers built to this one, because every change is backward compatible.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
OSPFv3 has no authentication of its own. When running over IPv6 it relies on the IP Authentication Header (RFC 4302) and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 4303), as described in RFC 4552, to ensure the integrity and the authentication or confidentiality of protocol packets. Protection against accidental data corruption is provided by the standard IPv6 upper-layer checksum, which covers the OSPF packet and a prepended pseudo-header.

Most OSPFv3 implementations run on systems that support multiple protocols with their own security domains. When IPsec is used, the implementation must check the IPsec Security Association and the local SA database, so that a packet authenticated with an association defined for another protocol on the same system is not accepted as OSPFv3. The RFC is explicit that these mechanisms do not protect against compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured routers: such routers can, accidentally or deliberately, cause malfunctions affecting the whole routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPFv3 does not lock its own messages. It uses IPv6's IPsec mechanisms for that, and an implementation must check that the security association belongs to OSPFv3. Even then, a broken or dishonest router inside the domain can still disrupt routing.

items.label: Router-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Describes a router's interfaces to the area.

items.label: Network-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Originated by the DR; lists routers on the link.

items.label: Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. A prefix outside the area but inside the AS.

items.label: Inter-Area-Router-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. A path to an AS boundary router.

items.label: AS-External-LSA
items.desc: AS scope. A prefix outside the AS.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: Previously used by MOSPF; may be reassigned.

items.label: NSSA-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. External prefix limited to one NSSA.

items.label: Link-LSA
items.desc: Link-local scope. Link-local address and prefixes of the link.

items.label: Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Prefixes tied to a router-LSA or network-LSA.
